newsitem.title: FRANCE: No big economic change seen from French right.
newsitem.headline: No big economic change seen from French right.

text.p: France's parliamentary election is unlikely to produce a radical shift from the existing policy of economic austerity and gradual state reform if the centre-right coalition gets back into power, economists said on Tuesday.

Although many of them expect the centre-right government to return to power after the two-round election on May 25 and June 1, they also believe it could be a close contest, since many voters may already decide they have had enough of cutbacks.

The chance of a more significant departure comes from the main opposition Socialist party, which argues the cutbacks are hurting growth and proposes government-supported job creation to counter record 12.8 percent unemployment.
As far as a brief campaign period is concerned, any stronger message than one of continuity from the current government could backfire into opposition hands, economists say.

And popular resentment, which has been one of the obstacles to current reform, would only be fuelled if a newly returned centre-right government changed took a far more free-market tack than promised, they say.

President Jacques Chirac's decision to call a snap election is seen primarily as an attempt to give the government a genuine mandate to cut public spending and slim the civil service, as it had been doing so far, perhaps with a more liberal touch.

"He (Chirac) is saying 'I need a very clear mandate', not necessarily more liberalism, but more legitimacy to do what we wanted to do in the first place," said Eric Muller, French economy specialist at UBS investment bank.
"He's not intending to introduce a pure liberal policy of the UK (British) style," said Philippe Brossard, economist in Paris for Dutch bank ABN Amro.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe's opening campaign speech on Tuesday lent credence to this argument. "Selfish individualism, vulgar capitalism and the simplist hyperliberalism of the 1980s are also out of fashion," Juppe said.

Chirac said when announcing the early elections that he was advancing the date by nine months because he wanted the French people "to express themselves clearly on the scale and speed of change over the next five years".

For the hardnosed analysts, the "five years" is as important as the "speed and scale of change", implying that Chirac is more frustrated by social unrest and trade union resistance to current policy than set on an abrupt divorce from France's traditional desire to avoid the excesses of free market rule.

The government is clearly faced with the need to tighten the belt further, mainly because it will have a tough time reining in the public deficit in 1998 to keep in line with the economic fitness criteria for European monetary union, economist say.

What it now wants to find a more effective combination of cutbacks in spending, which can hurt consumer confidence and therefore the spending needed to help growth, and tax cuts which are popular but hard to finance when the state needed to balance the budget deficit.
Economists say it is unclear who would be best placed, and most likely, to carry on Jean Arthuis's job as finance minister if indeed the centre-right coalition does get back into power.
Arthuis himself is seen as a candidate with a solid record to return to the job, but may be under some pressure.

Many say Alain Madelin, a firebrand liberal who is already on the campaign trail demanding a rolling back of the state, would have a hard time winning back a post from which he was ousted after a few months by Juppe after provoking trade unions.

Another name in the hat is Labour Minister Jacques Barrot, seen as a more consensual figure with a good track record in dealing with unions and soial security reform, but perhaps still lacking the weight needed for the finance ministry.

For both Barrot and Arthuis, however, newspapers say there is a threat both men could be put under judicial investigations into party funding scandals which might jeopardise their position. Both men deny any wrongdoing.
